decisions.title: Web hosting
decisions.body: Next.js is the web default. Vercel Pro runs it with every feature and no adapter. Cloudflare Workers (through the OpenNext adapter) is the best free host, and its free plan allows commercial use. Vercel's Hobby plan does not.

decisions.title: Getting paid
decisions.body: Selling software to customers in many countries: start with a merchant of record (Paddle), which collects and remits VAT and sales tax for you. Move to Stripe direct, with Stripe Tax, when you want lower fees and full control and can handle tax registrations yourself. Stripe is invite-only in some countries, including India; see the country notes.

decisions.title: Company formation
decisions.body: If you might raise venture money, the common default is a Delaware C-corp (Stripe Atlas or Clerky). Filing yourself is cheaper but not free: there is a state filing fee, a registered agent and annual franchise tax. If you won't raise, a local company in your own country is usually simpler. Country notes cover the UK, the EU and India.

decisions.title: Meeting notes
decisions.body: Granola for notes with no bot in the call, Fathom's free plan at zero budget. Health and other regulated data stay out of cloud note-takers unless the vendor signs the agreements you need.

decisions.title: One build workflow
decisions.body: The site's coding-agent stance is Claude Code. Use Superpowers for the plan, test and build loop, and Spec Kit only to write spec documents. Two planners in one repo give the agent conflicting instructions.

decisions.title: Jobs
decisions.body: A platform queue for fan-out and retries. A durable workflow engine (Inngest, or DBOS for free) for long, multi-step LLM jobs.

decisions.title: Newsletters
decisions.body: Your personal audience and your product's users are different lists: one tool each (see Personal brand and Sales + GTM).

decisions.title: Model APIs and customer data
decisions.body: Use a paid, no-training API tier for anything that touches customer data. Free tiers often allow human review or training on your inputs. Gemini's free tier also isn't allowed for apps serving users in the EU, Switzerland or the UK.

decisions.title: Healthcare clients
decisions.body: None of the free tiers in the default stack signs a HIPAA business associate agreement. AWS and Google Cloud let you accept one yourself; most SaaS vendors need a paid plan or a sales contract.

notes.title: Pin dependencies and actions
notes.body: LiteLLM had two separate supply-chain compromises in 2026: PyPI 1.82.7-1.82.8 in March, and v1.107.0 (PyPI and container images) on 21 October. Trivy's GitHub Action tags were hijacked in March. Pin packages and container digests, pin Actions to commit SHAs, and audit workflows with zizmor. If you installed an affected version, rotate every secret it could reach.

notes.title: Keep customer data off free AI tiers
notes.body: Free API tiers often allow training or human review, and some can't be used in the EU, Switzerland or the UK at all. Put customer and regulated data only on paid, no-training endpoints with the right agreements.

notes.title: Sandbox your coding agent
notes.body: Claude Code's Bash sandbox runs natively on macOS and Linux, and on Windows only inside WSL2. Prefer auto mode with allow and deny rules over skipping permission prompts, and open untrusted repositories inside a sandbox or dev container.

notes.title: Check licence terms at work
notes.body: Docker Desktop, OrbStack and some editors need a paid licence at companies above a size or revenue threshold, and some free tiers are personal-use only. Check before you standardise a team on them.

notes.title: Free tiers share quotas
notes.body: On most serverless free plans, every app in the account shares one request quota. Split noisy projects into separate accounts or move to the first paid tier when traffic grows.

phases.title: Set up your machine
steps: Install Claude Code; use auto mode with allow and deny rules instead of skipping permission prompts.
Set up your OS package manager (Homebrew on macOS, winget on Windows, your distro's on Linux) and a modern terminal.
Install the GitHub CLI and sign in: gh auth login.
Put secrets in a secrets manager, not in plaintext .env files.

phases.title: Claude Code core
steps: Add the official language-server plugins for your languages.
Choose one build workflow (Superpowers) and keep other planners out of the repo.
Add a browser tool for testing, a live-docs MCP and a web-search MCP.
Set a status line that shows usage limits and context.

phases.title: Accounts
steps: Create accounts for hosting, Postgres, auth, email, error tracking, analytics and uptime. Use the paid pick or the best free option from each Ship slot.
Register your domain and set up DNS and business email.
Get a production model API key on a no-training tier.

phases.title: Product stack
steps: Scaffold a TypeScript monorepo: Next.js, Hono, Drizzle on Postgres, Expo. Add Electron by hand if you need a desktop app.
Deploy the web app and API, and the MCP server if you have one.
Add tracing and evals in CI from day one.
Set up mobile builds and the app-store test tracks early; Play's closed-testing rule takes two weeks.

phases.title: Money and legal
steps: Form the company that fits your plans (see Decisions), open a business bank account and set up accounting.
Choose a merchant of record or Stripe, with tax handled.
Adopt standard contracts and e-signature, and publish a privacy policy that fits your users' countries.
Check your country's notes on tax registration and export invoicing with a professional.

phases.title: Sell
steps: Set up a CRM and prospecting data, and send from a separate warmed domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
Use one booking tool for interviews and sales calls, and a meeting-notes tool.
Ship a marketing site and docs with search consoles connected.
Add support, a feedback board and product demos when users arrive, then plan a launch.

phases.title: Run and grow
steps: Keep a notes system, a backlog and a calendar that protects focus time.
Post where your buyers are and keep a personal newsletter going.
Spend 45 minutes a week on the learning radar.
